title: The system: smart-meter telemetry ingest, where midnight outruns the validators
caption: Each layer has a bound and a policy for when it's reached: billing reads wait at the edge and are never lost, diagnostics are sampled or dropped, and consumers only take what they can finish.

steps.text: Meters report over the cellular network to edge gateways, one per tower. A gateway stores and forwards: it keeps every reading on local disk until the ingest API acknowledges it.

Two classes of data. Billing reads (the daily register plus 96 quarter-hour values) must never be lost. Diagnostics (voltage, signal strength, tamper events) can be sampled. The admission policy holds the bounds and quotas per class and reloads them live.
Billing reads are appended to a bounded, replicated log, and only then acknowledged, so the gateway can delete its copy. The bound is about an hour of validator throughput.
Diagnostics go to a separate bounded queue that drops its oldest entries when full; under load the sampler keeps 1 in 10 per meter.
Validators pull only as many batches as they have free slots, check for gaps and duplicates, and write idempotently to the time-series DB. Billing workers compute daily usage from it.
When the log nears its bound, the API answers 429 + Retry-After: the gateway keeps the data and tries later. Depth, consumer lag and shed counts go to monitoring.

scenarios.name: Midnight burst
scenarios.summary: Firmware sends the daily read at 00:00: 5 M batches in about two minutes against validators that finish 10k/s. The log absorbs it; diagnostics give way.

steps.text: At midnight 5 M meters send their billing batch within ~2 minutes: about 40 000 batches/s, 4× what the validators can finish.
The log's bound is an hour of work (36 M batches), so all 5 M are appended and acknowledged. Nothing waits at the edge.
Diagnostics keep arriving at ~5 000/s. With the log's lag above a minute, the policy turns on 1-in-10 sampling and the queue drops its oldest entries.
Validators drain the log at 10 000/s: 5 M ÷ 10k ≈ 500 s, so the night's reads are in the time-series DB about 8 minutes after midnight.

scenarios.name: Time-series DB slows
scenarios.summary: A compaction makes writes 5× slower during the midnight drain. Credits slow the validators by themselves; lag pushes back to the edge, and no billing read is lost.

steps.text: A compaction starts on the time-series DB; each write takes 5× longer.
Validator slots stay busy, so they pull less: throughput falls from 10 000 to 2 000 batches/s and the log's lag grows.
Lag passes 30 minutes. The policy stops admitting billing reads: 429 + Retry-After, and the gateways keep them on disk. Diagnostics are dropped at the queue.
Compaction ends, the lag drains, admission reopens, and the gateways replay with jitter. Every billing read arrives, just later; on-call sees the lag alert, not lost data.

scenarios.name: Firmware adds jitter
scenarios.summary: The cheapest capacity is load you never create: spread the daily read over four hours and the midnight peak almost disappears.

steps.text: An operator rolls out firmware that sends the daily read at a random minute between 00:00 and 04:00, derived from the meter id.
5 M batches ÷ 14 400 s ≈ 350/s instead of 40 000/s: about 100× lower at the peak.
The log's lag stays near zero, diagnostics are no longer sampled at night, and the validator fleet can shrink. The bounds stay: they still cover the next surprise.
